# Introduction

A first look at what the asymmetric contrasts do on **text**. The data is the
BBC news corpus analysed by Weine et al. ([arXiv
2601.05845](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.05845v1)) with the log1p link Poisson
NMF, so the factors found here can eventually be put next to theirs.

The counts are transformed with $\log(1 + X/s)$, where $s$ is the document
length divided by the mean document length, as in the log1p NMF analysis. The
columns are centred and the result whitened to $K = 80$ principal components.
**Three** contrasts are run on that whitening, so they are directly
comparable:

* $x|x|$, the asymmetric fastICA contrast used in the earlier analyses;
* $x^3/3$, the classical skewness contrast, of which $x|x| = x^2\,\text{sign}(x)$
  is a robustified version;
* EBproj with a **fixed exponential** prior ($\pi_0 = 0$,
  $c^2 = \sigma^2 = 1/2$, nothing estimated --- the `exp_fixed` configuration
  of
  [`code/fit_tgp_ebproj.R`](https://github.com/stephenslab/misc/blob/master/code/fit_tgp_ebproj.R)).
  Its loadings are the posterior means $M(U^Tw)$ rather than $U^Tw$ itself.

Everything is done three times: on the full data and on each half of a random
split of the documents, so that every maximum can be checked for
reproducibility.

The summary is that this works well, and that the three contrasts form a
resolution ladder. All three find clean, interpretable topics; they agree
almost exactly on the directions they share; and they differ mainly in how
far they keep splitting --- $x|x|$ finds 18 factors, `exp_fixed` 24 and
$x^3$ 36. Reproducibility runs the other way, so the choice among them is a
resolution-against-stability trade.

## The pipeline

The search for local maxima runs in three stages.

**Stage 1, the search**, independently in three *spaces* --- the full data and
each half, each with its own SVD and whitening --- and under each contrast, so
six searches. Each search is:

* five rank-$r$ fits at $r = K$ from different random starts. All $5K$ fits are then considered, duplicates among
  them are removed, and each distinct direction is then used to initialize the rank-1
  update.
* 1000 random rank-1 starts, run to convergence.

The resulting fits are then clustered at correlation 0.95.

**Stage 2, cross-contrast initialization.** Within each space, each contrast
is re-run starting from each of the *other contrasts'* maxima.

**Stage 3, cross-space initialization.** Within each contrast, each space is
re-run starting from each of the other two spaces' maxima. The spaces have
different whitenings, so a direction is carried through word space: the
whitened-space direction $w$ corresponds to the word-space vector
$g = V_{[,1:K]}\,\text{diag}(d_{1:K})\,w$, and the nearest direction in the
target's row space is $w' = \text{diag}(1/d)\,V^T g$, renormalized. This is
the transfer of
[`code/fit_immgent_ebproj_cross.R`](https://github.com/stephenslab/misc/blob/master/code/fit_immgent_ebproj_cross.R).

Stages 2 and 3 matter because a direction can be a genuine maximum in two
places and still be missed by one of the searches. Without these steps, "half 1 does
not have this factor" is ambiguous between "not a maximum there" and "a
maximum the search missed". 

## The data

The csv that `bbc_fig.R` in the `log1pNMF` repository reads is not distributed
with the package. It is a deduplicated copy of the original BBC news dataset of
[Greene and Cunningham (2006)](http://mlg.ucd.ie/datasets/bbc.html), which is
public, and was downloaded for this analysis from
[`http://mlg.ucd.ie/files/datasets/bbc-fulltext.zip`](http://mlg.ucd.ie/files/datasets/bbc-fulltext.zip)
(2.9 MB; SHA-256 `a351031a62325b3d7ff13146eeb035c22feca8290913b5183d1ff3be35109495`).
Taking the 2225 articles from that zip, dropping the 98
that are exact duplicates as plain text, and running their tokenisation
verbatim (SMART stopwords, Porter stemming, terms in more than four documents)
reproduces their matrix exactly: $2127 \times 5861$, with every one of their
5861 terms matched.

(One trap worth recording. The only non-ASCII content in the corpus is the
pound sign, as valid UTF-8, in 647 of the 2225 files. Run in a non-UTF-8
locale --- which is what `Rscript` gets when `LANG` is unset --- `tm` escapes
those bytes to the literal string `<c2><a3>`, which splits `£bn` into two junk
terms and leaves the escape text in every table downstream. `prep_bbc_data.R`
now forces a UTF-8 locale; without that the vocabulary is 5862 terms and only
5860 of theirs are matched.)

Compute is in
[`code/prep_bbc_data.R`](https://github.com/stephenslab/misc/blob/master/code/prep_bbc_data.R)
and
[`code/fit_bbc_ica.R`](https://github.com/stephenslab/misc/blob/master/code/fit_bbc_ica.R);
the whole pipeline takes about 90 seconds.

```{r load}
library(ggplot2)
library(fastTopics)

sps <- c("full", "half1", "half2")

name_by_words <- function(f)          # two leading words, as a factor label
  make.unique(apply(f$words$B, 1, function(b)
    paste(names(sort(b, decreasing = TRUE))[1:2], collapse = "/")))

label_fits <- function(x) {
  # Runs made before the contrast set became configurable have no $contrasts.
  if (is.null(x$contrasts)) x$contrasts <- names(x$fits$full)
  for (sp in sps) for (ct in x$contrasts) {
    f <- x$fits[[sp]][[ct]]
    colnames(f$L) <- colnames(f$G) <- rownames(f$words$B) <- name_by_words(f)
    x$fits[[sp]][[ct]] <- f
  }
  x
}

r   <- label_fits(readRDS("../output/bbc_ica_K80_scaled_3c.rds"))
cts <- r$contrasts
lab <- r$labels
get <- function(sp, ct) r$fits[[sp]][[ct]]

# The two contrasts that every run on this page has, for comparisons with the
# variants below, which were fitted before x^3 was added.
cts2 <- c("x|x|", "exp_fixed")

memb  <- function(L) { A <- pmax(L, 0); sweep(A, 2, apply(A, 2, max), "/") }
r2_by <- function(x, g)
  1 - sum(tapply(x, g, function(z) sum((z - mean(z))^2))) / sum((x - mean(x))^2)
top_words <- function(f, j, n = 12)
  paste(colnames(f$words$B)[order(-f$words$B[j, ])[1:n]], collapse = ", ")

# Cosine between the word-space directions of two fits.
cosmat <- function(fa, fb) crossprod(fa$G, fb$G)

# Mutual nearest neighbours: row i and column j match when j is i's nearest
# neighbour and i is j's. Returns, per row, its nearest column, the cosine,
# and whether the pairing is mutual.
mnn <- function(C) {
  a <- max.col(C, "first"); b <- max.col(t(C), "first"); i <- seq_len(nrow(C))
  data.frame(i = i, j = a, cos = C[cbind(i, a)], mutual = b[a] == i)
}

# Table formatting shared by the alignment tables below: a similarity is shown
# only where the pairing is mutual, "-" otherwise, and a mutual pair below the
# 0.7 cut is parenthesised.
fmt <- function(x) ifelse(is.na(x), "-",
                          ifelse(x > 0.7, sprintf("%.2f", x), sprintf("(%.2f)", x)))
pick <- function(nms, i) ifelse(is.na(i), "-", nms[pmax(i, 1)])

# Article headlines, used to name the documents a factor loads on.
hd <- readRDS("../data/bbc_dtm.rds")$headlines

# Raw projections U'w, unshrunken, for every contrast on the full data. For
# x|x| and x^3 these are the loadings; for exp_fixed the loadings are the
# posterior means, so this is the quantity before shrinkage.
U80 <- sqrt(r$spaces$full$n) * t(r$spaces$full$U_c[, 1:r$K])
Xraw <- lapply(cts, function(ct) {
  M <- crossprod(U80, get("full", ct)$W)
  colnames(M) <- colnames(get("full", ct)$L); M
})
names(Xraw) <- cts

# Standard reproducibility summary for one contrast of one run.
count_row <- function(g, ct) {
  fu <- g("full", ct); f1 <- g("half1", ct); f2 <- g("half2", ct)
  m1 <- mnn(cosmat(fu, f1)); m2 <- mnn(cosmat(fu, f2)); m12 <- mnn(cosmat(f1, f2))
  ok <- function(m) m$mutual & m$cos > 0.7
  c(full = ncol(fu$G), half1 = ncol(f1$G), half2 = ncol(f2$G),
    `full in both halves` = sum(ok(m1) & ok(m2)),
    `h1-h2 matched` = sum(ok(m12)), ceiling = min(ncol(f1$G), ncol(f2$G)),
    rate = round(sum(ok(m12)) / min(ncol(f1$G), ncol(f2$G)), 2))
}

# Full-data maxima, key words, and how each fares in the two halves.
factor_table <- function(g, ct) {
  fu <- g("full", ct); f1 <- g("half1", ct); f2 <- g("half2", ct)
  m1 <- mnn(cosmat(fu, f1)); m2 <- mnn(cosmat(fu, f2))
  data.frame(
    factor  = colnames(fu$L),
    half1   = fmt(ifelse(m1$mutual, m1$cos, NA)),
    half2   = fmt(ifelse(m2$mutual, m2$cos, NA)),
    in_both = ifelse(m1$mutual & m2$mutual &
                       pmin(m1$cos, m2$cos) > 0.7, "yes", ""),
    top_words = sapply(seq_len(ncol(fu$L)), function(j) top_words(fu, j, 10)))
}

# Align two fits that share a whitening, one row per factor.
pair_contrasts <- function(Xa, Xb, na, nb) {
  C <- cor(Xa, Xb); m <- mnn(C)
  ia <- ifelse(m$mutual, m$j, NA)
  lb <- setdiff(seq_len(ncol(C)), na.omit(ia))
  d <- data.frame(a = c(colnames(C[, 0, drop = FALSE]), rownames(C), rep("-", length(lb))),
                  b = c(pick(colnames(C), ia), colnames(C)[lb]),
                  cor = c(fmt(ifelse(m$mutual, m$cos, NA)), rep("-", length(lb))))
  names(d) <- c(na, nb, "cor")
  d
}
```

The corpus is small and the spectrum is flat. There is no elbow to cut at: after the first few components the eigenvalues decay smoothly. So choice of whitening dimension is a tricky judgement call. We tried $K=40,80$ and since $K=80$ seems to find a bit more real structure without "false positives" we present that first, with $K=40$ as an addendum.

```{r scree, fig.width=9, fig.height=3.4}
nshow <- 120
scree <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(r$spaces), function(nm)
  data.frame(space = nm, k = seq_len(nshow),
             eigenvalue = r$spaces[[nm]]$d[seq_len(nshow)]^2,
             pve = 100 * r$spaces[[nm]]$pve[seq_len(nshow)])))

p1 <- ggplot(scree, aes(k, pve, colour = space)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = r$K, colour = "firebrick") +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "component", y = "% of variance", colour = NULL,
       title = "Scree plot") + theme_bw()
p2 <- p1 + scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10() +
  labs(title = "Scree plot, log-log")
cowplot::plot_grid(p1 + theme(legend.position = "none"), p2, nrow = 1,
                   rel_widths = c(1, 1.3))
```


# Results: K = 80, three contrasts

## The search

The five rank-$r$ fits overlap but do not completely agree: of the 400
columns they produce, 185 ($x|x|$), 128 (`exp_fixed`) and 125 ($x^3$) are
distinct. Initializing at these does not add to the number of topics found.
Clustering results are insensitive to the choice of cutoff (threshold varied
between correlation 0.90 and 0.99).

```{r search-summary}
t(sapply(cts, function(ct) {
  f <- get("full", ct)
  c(`distinct rank-r` = f$n_rankr_distinct, `cut 0.90` = f$sens[1],
    `cut 0.95` = f$sens[2], `cut 0.99` = f$sens[3], maxima = ncol(f$W))
}))
```

### Cross-initialization adds nothing, anywhere

Stages 2 and 3 produce no additional maxima --- under no contrast and in no
space. Every direction transferred in, whether from another contrast or from
another space, relaxes onto a maximum the receiving search had already found.

```{r cross-summary}
z <- unlist(lapply(sps, function(sp) lapply(cts, function(ct)
  unlist(get(sp, ct)$n_cross))))
c(`transfers performed` = length(z), `new maxima found` = sum(z))
```

Thus, when a half does not have a factor, it is because the factor is not a
maximum of that half's objective, not because 1000 starts failed to find it.
The same applies across contrasts: a factor one contrast finds and another
does not is a genuine difference between the objectives.

### Maxima on the full data {.tabset}

```{r sizes, results='asis'}
for (ct in cts) {
  f <- get("full", ct); A <- memb(f$L)
  cat(sprintf("\n#### %s\n\n", ct))
  print(knitr::kable(data.frame(
    factor = colnames(f$L), from_random = f$n_random, from_rankr = f$n_from_rankr,
    docs_above_0.5 = colSums(A > 0.5),
    top_category = apply(A, 2, function(a)
      names(sort(tapply(a, lab, mean), decreasing = TRUE))[1]),
    R2_category = round(apply(A, 2, function(a) r2_by(a, lab)), 2)),
    row.names = FALSE,
    caption = "How each maximum was reached, and how it relates to the editorial categories"))
  cat("\n")
}
```

### {-}

## What the factors are

Word loadings come from regressing the centred $\log(1 + X/s)$ matrix on the
non-negative part of the document loadings (scaled to a maximum of 1) with an
intercept, as in
[`code/fit_immgent_ebproj.R`](https://github.com/stephenslab/misc/blob/master/code/fit_immgent_ebproj.R).
The `half1` and `half2` columns are the cosine to each half's mutual nearest
neighbour and `in_both` flags the factors that reproduce; those come from the
split analysed further down, and are repeated here so each factor can be read
off with its key words in one place.

### {.tabset}

```{r words, results='asis'}
for (ct in cts) {
  cat(sprintf("\n#### %s\n\n", ct))
  print(knitr::kable(factor_table(get, ct), row.names = FALSE,
    caption = "Full-data maxima, key words, and reproducibility in each half"))
  cat("\n")
}
```

### {-}

Every factor under every contrast is a recognisable topic, and none is a
nuisance axis: there is no document-length or vocabulary-size factor, which
is what dividing by $s$ and then applying a variance-stabilising transform is
supposed to achieve.

The three lists are nested rather than different. $x|x|$ finds 18: athletics
and doping, Yukos, computer security, takeover bids, the macroeconomy, party
politics, film awards, rugby, tennis, mobile phones, music, law and civil
liberties, football clubs, company results, television, video games,
corporate fraud, and developing-world aid. `exp_fixed` finds those and splits
six of them further --- doping from track championships, party competition
from the Blair/Brown government, the dollar and trade deficit from the
macroeconomy, digital music from music, the football match report from rugby,
and a box-office axis out of entertainment.

$x^3$ goes further again, to 36. Where `exp_fixed` has one tennis factor it
has two; where it has one rugby factor it has three; and it separates
business stories the others merge --- the LSE/Deutsche Börse bid, oil prices,
company results. The most striking addition is **`unit/club`**, led by
*"Shares rise on new Man Utd offer"*: the Glazer takeover, which appears in
the cross-cutting section below as the clearest example of a story the
editorial partition misfiles, is resolved by $x^3$ as a topic in its own
right.

## Structure plots

Documents grouped by their editorial category, memberships on the max-1
scale. The unnormalized panels keep the bar heights: a short bar is a
document that none of the factors explains.

```{r struct-fn}
# glasbey tops out at 32 colours and x^3 has 36 factors, so fall back to a
# generated palette when the list is longer.
factor_colours <- function(k) {
  if (k + 1 <= 32) return(Polychrome::glasbey.colors(k + 1)[-1])
  unname(Polychrome::createPalette(k, c("#5A5156", "#E4E1E3", "#F6222E"),
                                   M = 2000))
}

plot_struct <- function(A, normalize, title) {
  keep <- rowSums(A) > 0
  M <- A[keep, ]
  if (normalize) M <- M / rowSums(M)
  set.seed(1)   # structure_plot orders within each group by t-SNE
  structure_plot(M, grouping = droplevels(lab[keep]), gap = 20, verbose = FALSE,
                 colors = factor_colours(ncol(M))) +
    labs(y = "membership", fill = NULL,
         title = sprintf("%s: %d maxima, %s%s", title, ncol(M),
                         if (normalize) "normalized" else "unnormalized",
                         if (all(keep)) "" else
                           sprintf(" - %d document(s) dropped", sum(!keep)))) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(size = 9),
          legend.text = element_text(size = 6),
          legend.key.size = unit(0.3, "cm"))
}
```

### {.tabset}

```{r struct, results='asis', fig.width=10, fig.height=4}
for (ct in cts) for (nz in c(TRUE, FALSE)) {
  cat(sprintf("\n#### %s, %s\n\n", ct, if (nz) "normalized" else "unnormalized"))
  print(plot_struct(memb(get("full", ct)$L), nz, ct))
  cat("\n")
}
```

### {-}

The unnormalized panels separate the three
contrasts more clearly than the factor lists do.

```{r struct-stats}
t(sapply(cts, function(ct) {
  A <- memb(get("full", ct)$L)
  c(factors = ncol(A), `median total membership` = round(median(rowSums(A)), 2),
    `docs explained by nothing` = sum(rowSums(A) < 0.1),
    `median docs above 0.5` = median(colSums(A > 0.5)))
}))
```

Under $x|x|$ and `exp_fixed` the decomposition is sparse in the documents ---
most bars are well short of 1, and `exp_fixed` leaves 172 documents, 8% of
the corpus, with essentially nothing on them. $x^3$ is different: with 36
narrow factors the median total membership rises above 1 and **no** document
is left unexplained. So the resolution ladder is also a coverage ladder.

## Do the contrasts agree?

Comparison on the **raw projections** $U^Tw$, unshrunken on all three sides
--- `exp_fixed`'s reported loadings are posterior means, and the shrinkage
attenuates correlations that are otherwise near 1.

```{r agree-summary}
t(sapply(list(c("x|x|", "exp_fixed"), c("x|x|", "x^3"), c("exp_fixed", "x^3")),
         function(pr) {
  m <- mnn(cor(Xraw[[pr[1]]], Xraw[[pr[2]]]))
  c(`factors, first` = ncol(Xraw[[pr[1]]]), `factors, second` = ncol(Xraw[[pr[2]]]),
    `mutual pairs` = sum(m$mutual), `median r` = round(median(m$cos[m$mutual]), 3),
    `pairs above 0.9` = sum(m$mutual & m$cos > 0.9))
})) |> `rownames<-`(c("x|x| vs exp_fixed", "x|x| vs x^3", "exp_fixed vs x^3"))
```

The three are not finding different structure. Every $x|x|$ factor has an
`exp_fixed` partner at a median correlation of 0.980; `exp_fixed` and $x^3$
agree even more closely, 23 of 24 pairs at 0.983. They are finding the same
structure at three resolutions, and each contrast in turn keeps splitting
after the previous one has stopped.

### {.tabset}

```{r agree-tables, results='asis'}
for (pr in list(c("x|x|", "exp_fixed"), c("exp_fixed", "x^3"))) {
  cat(sprintf("\n#### %s vs %s\n\n", pr[1], pr[2]))
  print(knitr::kable(pair_contrasts(Xraw[[pr[1]]], Xraw[[pr[2]]], pr[1], pr[2]),
    row.names = FALSE, caption = "One row per factor, paired by mutual nearest neighbour"))
  cat("\n")
}
```

### {-}

Thirteen of the 36 $x^3$ factors have no `exp_fixed` counterpart, and they
are all genuine extra resolution: the Man Utd takeover, a second tennis
factor, oil prices, broadband, UKIP, public-sector pensions, EU patent law,
film festivals, the Budget, search engines, DVD technology, France/Wales
rugby, and games in schools. Going the other way, only one `exp_fixed`
factor, `band/album`, has no $x^3$ partner.

### Where the contrasts differ, and by how much

```{r raw-scatter, fig.width=10, fig.height=9}
mr  <- mnn(cor(Xraw[["x|x|"]], Xraw[["exp_fixed"]]))
ord <- order(mr$cos)
pd <- do.call(rbind, lapply(ord, function(i) data.frame(
  xx = Xraw[["x|x|"]][, i], ef = Xraw[["exp_fixed"]][, mr$j[i]], category = lab,
  panel = sprintf("%s  /  %s\nr = %.3f", colnames(Xraw[["x|x|"]])[i],
                  colnames(Xraw[["exp_fixed"]])[mr$j[i]], mr$cos[i]))))
pd$panel <- factor(pd$panel, levels = unique(pd$panel))

ggplot(pd, aes(ef, xx, colour = category)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(size = 0.4, alpha = 0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, ncol = 4, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "exp_fixed,  U'w (unshrunken)", y = "x|x|,  U'w", colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 6.5), legend.position = "bottom",
        axis.text = element_text(size = 6))
```

```{r raw-skew}
skew <- function(x) mean(x^3) / sd(x)^3
data.frame(
  `x|x|` = colnames(Xraw[["x|x|"]]),
  exp_fixed = colnames(Xraw[["exp_fixed"]])[mr$j],
  r = round(mr$cos, 3),
  `skew, x|x|` = round(apply(Xraw[["x|x|"]], 2, skew), 2),
  `skew, exp_fixed` = round(apply(Xraw[["exp_fixed"]], 2, skew)[mr$j], 2),
  check.names = FALSE)[ord, ] |> knitr::kable(row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "x|x| against exp_fixed on the raw projections, worst-matching pairs first")
```

Panels are ordered worst match first. The bulk of documents sits in a tight
blob near the origin and falls exactly on the diagonal, and the two contrasts
agree completely about which documents are in the long positive tail. Where
they disagree is the *near* tail --- the middling documents at 2 to 5 ---
which `exp_fixed` pushes out slightly further. That shows up as skewness:
`exp_fixed`'s direction is more skewed than $x|x|$'s in **every** pair
without exception, though usually only slightly (median 3.99 against 3.84).

The one substantially different pair is `countri/world` against
`countri/aid` at 0.820, and the disagreement there is one-sided: 25 documents
are strongly positive on both, six on $x|x|$ alone, and none on `exp_fixed`
alone. The six are not tsunami stories --- *"Radcliffe yet to answer GB
call"*, *"Kenya lift Chepkemei's suspension"*, *"GB quartet get cross country
call"* --- so the $x|x|$ version of this factor has picked up African and
international distance running through `countri`, `world` and `nation`, while
the EBproj version stays on the tsunami and aid story. That is the only pair
where two contrasts resolve a topic differently rather than by degree, and
there the exponential prior gives the cleaner factor.

## Reproducibility across halves

Each half has its own SVD, whitening and search, and stage 3 has already
carried every maximum into every other space, so what follows is about the
objectives and not about the search. Factors are compared in word space, the
only representation the three fits share. (Correlating the fitted
word-loading vectors $B$ instead picks the same partner for every factor
whose best match is above 0.6 and agrees with the cosine to within 0.07 on
those, so nothing below hinges on the choice of metric.)

### When are two factors the same?

Pooling the three comparisons (half 1 vs half 2, full vs each half) and all
three contrasts, here is every pairwise cosine, first all together and then
split by whether the pair are mutual nearest neighbours.

```{r cos-dist, fig.width=9, fig.height=3.2}
pairs_all <- do.call(rbind, lapply(cts, function(ct)
  do.call(rbind, lapply(list(c("half1", "half2"), c("full", "half1"),
                             c("full", "half2")), function(pr) {
    C <- cosmat(get(pr[1], ct), get(pr[2], ct))
    m <- mnn(C)
    is_p <- matrix(FALSE, nrow(C), ncol(C))
    is_p[cbind(m$i[m$mutual], m$j[m$mutual])] <- TRUE
    data.frame(cos = as.vector(C),
               kind = ifelse(as.vector(is_p), "mutual nearest neighbours",
                             "all other pairs"))
  }))))
both <- transform(pairs_all, kind = "all pairs together")

ggplot(rbind(both, pairs_all), aes(cos)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.05, boundary = 0, fill = "grey35") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.7, colour = "firebrick") +
  facet_wrap(~ factor(kind, c("all pairs together",
                              "mutual nearest neighbours",
                              "all other pairs")), scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "cosine between word-space directions", y = "pairs") +
  theme_bw()
```

The combined histogram is bimodal: a large mode at zero decaying through
0.5, a trough between 0.65 and 0.80, and a second mode above 0.85. Split
apart, neither component is bimodal on its own --- the non-partner pairs
decay smoothly from zero, the mutual pairs are unimodal with the mode
against 1 and a thin tail reaching down. The tail is what a threshold is
for: a factor with no real counterpart still has a nearest neighbour, and if
its counterpart is equally orphaned the two pair up regardless.

```{r cos-quantiles}
np <- pairs_all$cos[pairs_all$kind != "mutual nearest neighbours"]
mp <- pairs_all$cos[pairs_all$kind == "mutual nearest neighbours"]
rbind(`non-partner pairs` = c(n = length(np),
        round(quantile(np, c(.95, .99, .995, 1)), 2)),
      `mutual pairs`      = c(n = length(mp),
        round(quantile(mp, c(.05, .1, .5, 1)), 2)))
```

The null agrees with the antimode: non-partner cosines reach 0.66 at their
99.5th percentile. **The criterion used throughout is mutual nearest
neighbour plus cosine > 0.7**, which sits in the trough of the combined
distribution and just above the 99.5th percentile of the null.

### The result

```{r half-summary}
t(sapply(cts, function(ct) count_row(get, ct)))
```

**Resolution and reproducibility pull in opposite directions.** The
half-to-half match rate --- the fraction of the maximum possible pairs that
match, and the most demanding of these measures --- falls monotonically as
the contrasts get finer: 0.75 for $x|x|$, 0.64 for `exp_fixed`, 0.31 for
$x^3$. Against the full data rather than between the halves, $x^3$ still has
the most reproducible factors in absolute terms (19, against 16 and 14), but
that is barely half its list.

The reason is visible in the contrasts themselves. $x^3$ weights a loading
by its cube, so a direction is rewarded for a few very large values much
more strongly than $x|x|$, which weights by the square. That is what lets it
isolate a topic carried by ten documents, and also what makes the particular
ten depend on the sample.

### All three fits side by side {.tabset}

One row per topic, aligning the full data and the two halves. Rows are
anchored on the full-data maxima; any half factor that no full-data factor
claims gets its own row at the bottom, paired with its own mutual nearest
neighbour in the other half where it has one. The `h1-h2` column is the
cosine between the two half factors on that row --- reported, but not
required for `in_both`, which uses the same rule as the summary above.

```{r half-detail, results='asis'}
consolidate <- function(ct) {
  fu <- get("full", ct); f1 <- get("half1", ct); f2 <- get("half2", ct)
  m1 <- mnn(cosmat(fu, f1)); m2 <- mnn(cosmat(fu, f2))
  C12 <- cosmat(f1, f2); m12 <- mnn(C12)
  i1 <- ifelse(m1$mutual, m1$j, NA); i2 <- ifelse(m2$mutual, m2$j, NA)
  c1 <- ifelse(m1$mutual, m1$cos, NA); c2 <- ifelse(m2$mutual, m2$cos, NA)

  l1 <- setdiff(seq_len(ncol(f1$L)), na.omit(i1))
  l2 <- setdiff(seq_len(ncol(f2$L)), na.omit(i2))
  j1 <- ifelse(m12$mutual[l1] & m12$j[l1] %in% l2, m12$j[l1], NA)
  l2 <- setdiff(l2, na.omit(j1))
  x1 <- c(l1, rep(NA, length(l2))); x2 <- c(j1, l2)

  d <- data.frame(
    full  = c(colnames(fu$L), rep("-", length(x1))),
    half1 = c(pick(colnames(f1$L), i1), pick(colnames(f1$L), x1)),
    half2 = c(pick(colnames(f2$L), i2), pick(colnames(f2$L), x2)),
    `full-h1` = fmt(c(c1, rep(NA, length(x1)))),
    `full-h2` = fmt(c(c2, rep(NA, length(x2)))),
    `h1-h2` = fmt(c(ifelse(is.na(i1) | is.na(i2), NA,
                           C12[cbind(pmax(i1, 1), pmax(i2, 1))]),
                    ifelse(is.na(x1) | is.na(x2), NA,
                           C12[cbind(pmax(x1, 1), pmax(x2, 1))]))),
    check.names = FALSE)
  d$in_both <- ifelse(d$half1 != "-" & d$half2 != "-" &
                        !grepl("\\(", paste(d$`full-h1`, d$`full-h2`)),
                      "yes", "")
  d
}
for (ct in cts) {
  cat(sprintf("\n#### %s\n\n", ct))
  print(knitr::kable(consolidate(ct), row.names = FALSE,
    caption = "Every maximum across the three fits, one row per topic"))
  cat("\n")
}
```

### {-}

# Follow-up: cross-cutting factors at K = 80

The editorial categories are a crude partition --- a story about the
Manchester United takeover is filed under Sport but is a business story --- so
a useful question about any decomposition is whether it finds topics that cut
across them. This section looks for those in the $K = 80$ `exp_fixed` fit.

Nothing here uses the labels to fit anything; they are only used to describe
what the factors turn out to contain.

```{r xc-setup}
efx <- get("full", "exp_fixed")
Ax  <- memb(efx$L)

# A factor's "home" category is the commonest among its 30 strongest
# documents; the mix over those 30 is how cross-cutting it is.
topN <- 30
mixtab <- sapply(seq_len(ncol(Ax)), function(j)
  table(lab[order(-Ax[, j])[1:topN]]))
rownames(mixtab) <- levels(lab)
share <- sweep(mixtab, 2, colSums(mixtab), "/")
home  <- levels(lab)[apply(share, 2, which.max)]
ent   <- apply(share, 2, function(p) { p <- p[p > 0]; -sum(p * log(p)) })
```

## Which factors cut across categories

```{r xc-table}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  factor = colnames(Ax), home = home,
  categories = colSums(mixtab > 0),
  `largest share` = round(apply(share, 2, max), 2),
  entropy = round(ent, 2),
  mix = apply(share, 2, function(p)
    paste(sprintf("%s %.0f%%", levels(lab)[p > 0], 100 * p[p > 0]),
          collapse = ", ")),
  check.names = FALSE)[order(-ent), ], row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Editorial categories of the 30 strongest documents on each factor")
```

Most factors are almost perfectly category-pure: sixteen of the 24 draw all
30 of their strongest documents from a single category. That is reassuring
rather than disappointing --- nobody told the method the categories exist ---
but it means the interesting cases are few, and they are of two kinds.

**One factor is genuinely cross-cutting.** `countri/aid` (`countri, aid,
tsunami, disast, debt, world, nation, relief`) draws its top 30 from four
categories: half Business, over a third Politics, and a scattering of
Entertainment and Tech. The Indian Ocean tsunami was simultaneously a
disaster-relief story, a debt-and-aid story, a government story and a
charity-telethon story, and the factor spans all of those. It is the one
place where the decomposition clearly identifies a subject the editorial
partition splits up.

**One is a two-category topic.** `music/digit` (`music, digit, file,
download, industri, share, peer, legal`) is 80% Tech and 20% Entertainment:
legal downloading sits on the boundary by construction.

## Documents filed under one category, loading on another's topic

The more common pattern is not a factor that spans categories but a factor
with a clear home and a handful of documents from elsewhere that belong to it
anyway. These are the individual stories the editorial partition misfiles.
The table below is restricted to the 22 factors that do have a home --- at
least 80% of their top 30 from one category --- since for `countri/aid` and
`music/digit` an out-of-category document is the normal case rather than the
exception.

```{r xc-offcat}
# Only factors with a real home: at least 80% of the top 30 from one
# category. The two cross-cutting factors above are excluded by construction
# -- a document from "another" category is not surprising for a factor that
# does not belong to one in the first place.
concentrated <- apply(share, 2, max) > 0.8
off <- do.call(rbind, lapply(which(concentrated), function(j) {
  i <- which(Ax[, j] > 0.4 & lab != home[j])
  if (!length(i)) return(NULL)
  i <- i[order(-Ax[i, j])][1:min(3, length(i))]
  data.frame(factor = colnames(Ax)[j], home = home[j],
             filed_under = as.character(lab[i]),
             membership = round(Ax[i, j], 2), headline = hd[i])
}))
knitr::kable(off[order(-off$membership), ], row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Documents loading above 0.4 on a concentrated factor from outside its home category")
```

The clearest example of the kind is **`bid/offer`**, the takeover factor
(`bid, offer, share, deutsch, takeov, lse, boers, sharehold`), whose home is
Business and
whose strongest outside document is *"Ferdinand casts doubt over Glazer"*,
filed under Sport --- the Glazer bid for Manchester United, a takeover story
that happens to be about a football club. *"Tottenham bid £8m for Forest
duo"* comes next, which is the same word bag applied to transfer fees.

Others worth naming:

* **`mobil/phone`** (Tech) picks up *"MPs issued with Blackberry threat"*
  (Politics) and *"Brussels raps mobile call charges"* (Business) --- the
  regulatory and parliamentary side of a technology topic.
* **`game/consol`** (Tech) picks up *"Game warnings 'must be clearer'"*
  (Politics), a classification-and-regulation story, and *"News Corp eyes
  video games market"* (Business). That last headline appears twice: the
  corpus contains two near-identical versions of the story whose text differs
  slightly, so only exact duplicates were removed in the preparation.
* **`show/bbc`** (Entertainment) picks up *"UK net users leading TV
  downloads"* (Tech) and *"'Poll Idols' face first hurdles"* (Politics), the
  latter about reality-TV formats applied to elections.

## Documents that bridge two topics

The same thing seen document-first: articles loading above 0.3 on factors
whose home categories differ.

```{r xc-bridge}
dom <- home
br <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(Ax)), function(i) {
  j <- which(Ax[i, ] > 0.3)
  if (length(j) < 2 || length(unique(dom[j])) < 2) return(NULL)
  data.frame(filed_under = as.character(lab[i]), headline = hd[i],
             factors = paste(sprintf("%s [%s] %.2f", colnames(Ax)[j],
                                     dom[j], Ax[i, j]), collapse = "; "))
}))
knitr::kable(head(br[order(-nchar(br$factors)), ], 15), row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Documents loading on factors with different home categories")
```

## A caveat: not every crossing is real

Sorting sport documents by their largest loading on a non-sport factor shows
the failure mode as well as the successes.

```{r xc-sport}
sp <- which(lab == "Sports"); ns <- which(dom != "Sports")
b  <- apply(Ax[sp, ns, drop = FALSE], 1, function(a) c(which.max(a), max(a)))
o  <- order(-b[2, ])[1:8]
knitr::kable(data.frame(headline = hd[sp[o]], factor = colnames(Ax)[ns[b[1, o]]],
                        home = dom[ns[b[1, o]]], membership = round(b[2, o], 2)),
             row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Sport documents and their strongest non-sport factor")
```

The top entry, the Glazer story on `bid/offer`, is a genuine crossing. The
next few are not: *"Moya fights back for Indian title"* loads 0.40 on
`countri/aid` because of `indian`, and *"Sydney to host north v south game"*
and the Lions tour stories load on it through `world`, `nation` and
`countri`. So the method is finding shared *vocabulary*, which is usually but
not always shared *subject*. At memberships below about 0.4 on this data the
crossings should be read as word overlap unless the headline says otherwise.

# Addendum: K = 40

The same pipeline at $K = 40$, all three contrasts, everything else
unchanged. It was the main analysis in an earlier version of this page and
is kept because it makes the resolution-against-stability trade very clear.

```{r k40-load}
r40 <- label_fits(readRDS("../output/bbc_ica_K40_scaled_3c.rds"))
get40 <- function(sp, ct) r40$fits[[sp]][[ct]]
```

```{r k40-counts}
tab <- rbind(t(sapply(cts, function(ct) count_row(get, ct))),
             t(sapply(cts, function(ct) count_row(get40, ct))))
rownames(tab) <- sprintf("K=%d, %s", rep(c(80, 40), each = length(cts)), cts)
tab
```

Halving $K$ costs factors under every contrast --- 18 to 15, 24 to 18, 36 to
20 --- and buys a large amount of stability: the half-to-half match rate goes
from 0.75 to 0.92 for $x|x|$, 0.64 to 0.88 for `exp_fixed`, and 0.31 to 0.75
for $x^3$. At $K = 40$ even the cubic contrast is more reproducible than
$x|x|$ was at $K = 80$.

Cross-initialization adds nothing here either, and adding $x^3$ to the
$K = 40$ run leaves the other two contrasts bit-identical to the
two-contrast fit, exactly as at $K = 80$.

$K = 40$ is a coarsening rather than a different answer: every $K = 40$
factor is a mutual nearest neighbour of a $K = 80$ factor under the same
contrast.

```{r k40-vs-k80, results='asis'}
for (ct in cts) {
  a <- get40("full", ct); b <- get("full", ct); m <- mnn(cosmat(a, b))
  cat(sprintf("\n- **%s**: %d of %d $K = 40$ factors matched, median cosine %.2f\n",
              ct, sum(m$mutual), ncol(a$G), median(m$cos[m$mutual])))
}
```

So if the aim is a decomposition whose factors will still be there in a fresh
sample, $K = 40$ is the better operating point at any of the three contrasts.
If the aim is to enumerate candidate topics for inspection, $K = 80$ with
$x^3$ finds roughly twice as many, and the half-split says which to trust.

# Follow-up: a small pseudo-count, $\log(0.001 + X/s)$

Everything above uses $\log(1 + X/s)$. The log1p NMF of Weine et al. carries a
pseudo-count $c$ and their headline BBC fit uses $c = 0.001$, so this section
runs the identical pipeline on $\log(c + X/s)$ at $c = 0.001$, at $K = 80$
and, for reference, at $K = 40$.

Note first that the pseudo-count only rescales and shifts:
$$\log(c + z) = \log(c) + \log(1 + z/c),$$
and the constant disappears in the column centring. So $\log(0.001 + X/s)$ and
$\log(1 + X/(0.001\,s))$ give exactly the same whitening --- the two readings of
"$c$" coincide --- and the sparse form $\log(1 + z/c)$ is what is computed.
What $c$ actually controls is how much the transform flattens the non-zero
counts relative to the zeros. At $c = 0.001$ a count of 1 maps to about 6.9
and a count of 2 to 7.6, so the gap between absent and present dwarfs every
gap between one occurrence and many: the analysis is close to
presence/absence.

```{r c0-load}
rc <- lapply(c(`K = 40` = "bbc_ica_K40_scaled_c0.001",
               `K = 80` = "bbc_ica_K80_scaled_c0.001"),
             function(stem) label_fits(readRDS(sprintf("../output/%s.rds", stem))))
getc <- function(k) function(sp, ct) rc[[k]]$fits[[sp]][[ct]]
```

### The topics are coherent, and coarser

They are. Every $K = 80$ factor under both contrasts is a recognisable topic,
with no nuisance axis --- in particular none of the `number/top` box-office
oddity that $c = 1$ threw up at this rank. The factors are also *broader*:
`x|x|` finds 14 rather than 18 and `exp_fixed` 18 rather than 24, and what
disappears is the finer splits. Television goes under both contrasts; $x|x|$
additionally loses corporate results, video games and the WorldCom fraud,
while `exp_fixed` loses the dollar and trade deficit, digital music, the
Chelsea-specific football factor and the `number/top` box-office axis. The
survivors are the large subject areas.

They are not different factors, though. Matched in word space, all 14 of the
$K = 80$ $x|x|$ factors and 17 of the 18 `exp_fixed` factors are mutual
nearest neighbours of a $c = 1$ factor at the same rank, median cosine 0.94
to 0.95 --- so with one exception nothing at $c = 0.001$ is new. The small
pseudo-count coarsens the decomposition rather than reorienting it. (The
exception, `exp_fixed`'s `parti/elect`, is the UKIP and Kilroy-Silk factor,
which $c = 1$ splits differently.)

```{r c0-vs-c1, results='asis'}
for (ct in cts2) {
  a <- get("full", ct); b <- getc("K = 80")("full", ct)
  m <- mnn(cosmat(b, a))
  print(knitr::kable(data.frame(
    `c = 0.001` = colnames(b$L),
    `c = 1`     = pick(colnames(a$L), ifelse(m$mutual, m$j, NA)),
    cos         = fmt(ifelse(m$mutual, m$cos, NA)), check.names = FALSE),
    row.names = FALSE,
    caption = sprintf("K = 80, %s: the c = 0.001 factors against the c = 1 factors", ct)))
  cat("\n")
}
```

The two contrasts still agree almost perfectly with each other at
$c = 0.001$: 12 of 13 mutual pairs at $K = 40$ and 13 of 14 at $K = 80$,
median cosine 0.94--0.96.

### But they reproduce worse

This is the part that argues against the small pseudo-count. Across both
ranks and both contrasts, the fraction of possible half-to-half pairs that
match drops sharply.

```{r c0-counts}
rbind(`K=40 c=1,     x|x|`      = count_row(get40, "x|x|"),
      `K=40 c=1,     exp_fixed` = count_row(get40, "exp_fixed"),
      `K=40 c=0.001, x|x|`      = count_row(getc("K = 40"), "x|x|"),
      `K=40 c=0.001, exp_fixed` = count_row(getc("K = 40"), "exp_fixed"),
      `K=80 c=1,     x|x|`      = count_row(get, "x|x|"),
      `K=80 c=1,     exp_fixed` = count_row(get, "exp_fixed"),
      `K=80 c=0.001, x|x|`      = count_row(getc("K = 80"), "x|x|"),
      `K=80 c=0.001, exp_fixed` = count_row(getc("K = 80"), "exp_fixed"))
```

At $K = 40$ the half-to-half match rate falls from 0.92 to 0.62 under $x|x|$
and from 0.88 to 0.57 under `exp_fixed`; at $K = 80$ from 0.75 to 0.57 and
from 0.64 to 0.56. Both the numerator and the denominator shrink, so this is
not an artefact of finding fewer factors --- the factors that *are* found hold
up less well. The whitening is also slightly less efficient: 40 PCs carry
18.9% of the variance at $c = 0.001$ against 21.4% at $c = 1$, and 80 PCs
27.4% against 30.4%.

Cross-initialization again adds nothing at either rank, so this is a property
of the objectives and not of the search.

```{r c0-cross}
z <- unlist(lapply(names(rc), function(k) lapply(sps, function(sp)
  lapply(cts2, function(ct) unlist(getc(k)(sp, ct)$n_cross)))))
c(`transfers performed` = length(z), `new maxima found` = sum(z))
```

So $c = 0.001$ buys nothing here. It gives a coarser view of the same
structure --- fewer factors, all of them matching $c = 1$ factors, none of
them new --- and it makes that structure less reproducible. Pushing the
transform towards presence/absence throws away the information in *how often*
a word appears, and on this corpus that information is evidently what makes
the maxima stable. $\log(1 + X/s)$ remains the better choice.

### The factors {.tabset}

```{r c0-factors, results='asis'}
for (ct in cts2) {
  cat(sprintf("\n#### %s\n\n", ct))
  print(knitr::kable(factor_table(getc("K = 80"), ct), row.names = FALSE,
    caption = "K = 80, c = 0.001: full-data maxima, key words, and reproducibility"))
  cat("\n")
}
```

### {-}

# Follow-up: searching over words instead of documents

Everything so far searches for sparse directions over **documents**: a factor
is a set of articles, and its words come afterwards from a regression. The
transpose is equally well defined --- search the row space instead, so that a
factor is a sparse set of **words** and the documents come from the
regression. $K = 80$, $\log(1 + X/s)$, both contrasts, the same document
half-split, everything else unchanged (`BBC_SPACE=words` in
[`code/fit_bbc_ica.R`](https://github.com/stephenslab/misc/blob/master/code/fit_bbc_ica.R)).

**The centring has to be transposed too**, and this is not a detail. The
contrasts and the centred priors assume the loadings they see are mean zero.
Centring the columns makes every column of $X_c$ sum to zero over documents,
so the column space is orthogonal to $\mathbf{1}_n$ and every *document*
loading is mean zero --- right for the document search. For the word search
the *rows* must be centred instead, so that the same holds in $\mathbb{R}^p$.
On this data, row-centring puts the mean of each word-space singular vector
at $4\times10^{-18}$ while column-centring leaves it at $4\times10^{-4}$; run
the word search on the column-centred matrix and the all-ones word direction
stays inside the space being searched, and the contrasts duly report
overall-word-frequency axes (`year, time, make, work, run`) as factors.

One simplification does fall out of word mode: every fit lives in the same
5861-dimensional word space, so half-to-half comparison is direct and the
$V\,\text{diag}(d)\,w$ transfer is not needed.

```{r words-load}
rw <- readRDS("../output/bbc_ica_K80_scaled_words.rds")
getw <- function(sp, ct) rw$fits[[sp]][[ct]]
# In word mode the loadings are per word, so a factor names itself.
for (sp in sps) for (ct in names(rw$fits$full)) {
  f <- rw$fits[[sp]][[ct]]
  colnames(f$L) <- colnames(f$G) <-
    make.unique(apply(f$L, 2, function(x)
      paste(rownames(f$L)[order(-x)[1:2]], collapse = "/")))
  rw$fits[[sp]][[ct]] <- f
}
```

## The two contrasts behave very differently here

```{r words-counts}
rbind(`documents, x|x|`      = count_row(get, "x|x|"),
      `documents, exp_fixed` = count_row(get, "exp_fixed"),
      `words, x|x|`          = count_row(getw, "x|x|"),
      `words, exp_fixed`     = count_row(getw, "exp_fixed"))
```

Over documents the two contrasts found 18 and 24 factors and agreed with each
other almost perfectly. Over words they diverge: $x|x|$ finds 15, close to
its document-space count, while `exp_fixed` collapses to 10 on the full data
and to 7 and 5 in the halves. Cross-initialization adds nothing in either
case, and the clustering is insensitive to the cut, so the collapse is a
property of the objective in this space rather than a search failure.

Why the exponential prior should do so much worse over words than over
documents is not obvious. One guess: the word marginals are far more
skewed than the document marginals --- a handful of words appear everywhere
and most appear in a handful of documents --- so a prior with a fixed scale
$c^2 = 1/2$ is a much worse description of a word loading than of a document
loading. Estimating $c$ (the `exp` configuration) would test that.

## The factors {.tabset}

Each factor with its strongest words, how it fares in the two halves, and the
article that loads on it most, from the regression of documents on the word
memberships.

```{r words-factors, results='asis'}
for (ct in cts2) {
  f <- getw("full", ct); A <- memb(f$L)
  m1 <- mnn(cosmat(f, getw("half1", ct))); m2 <- mnn(cosmat(f, getw("half2", ct)))
  top <- apply(f$words$B, 1, which.max)
  cat(sprintf("\n### %s\n\n", ct))
  print(knitr::kable(data.frame(
    factor = colnames(f$L), `words > 0.5` = colSums(A > 0.5),
    half1 = fmt(ifelse(m1$mutual, m1$cos, NA)),
    half2 = fmt(ifelse(m2$mutual, m2$cos, NA)),
    top_words = sapply(seq_len(ncol(f$L)), function(j)
      paste(rownames(f$L)[order(-f$L[, j])[1:9]], collapse = ", ")),
    leading_document = hd[top],
    filed_under = as.character(lab[top]), check.names = FALSE),
    row.names = FALSE,
    caption = "Word-space maxima: strongest words, reproducibility, and leading article"))
  cat("\n")
}
```

## {-}

The $x|x|$ factors are mostly recognisable topics --- tennis, the
macroeconomy, party politics, video games, music charts, film awards, mobile
phones, doping, athletics, Yukos, share dealing, computer security, company
results --- and each picks out a sensible leading article. Two are not: a
`year/work` axis that no half reproduces, and `year/open`, which is a second
copy of tennis. Note also how many factors have `year` among their top two
words; with the rows centred, `year` behaves as a high-frequency word that
co-varies with almost everything, and it tends to ride along.

## Against the document-space factors

Both searches produce word-space directions --- explicitly in word mode, as
$V\,\text{diag}(d)\,w$ in document mode --- so they match directly.

```{r words-vs-docs, results='asis'}
for (ct in cts2) {
  a <- getw("full", ct); b <- get("full", ct); m <- mnn(cosmat(a, b))
  print(knitr::kable(data.frame(
    `word space` = colnames(a$L),
    `document space` = pick(colnames(b$L), ifelse(m$mutual, m$j, NA)),
    cos = fmt(ifelse(m$mutual, m$cos, NA)), check.names = FALSE),
    row.names = FALSE,
    caption = sprintf("%s: word-space factors against document-space factors", ct)))
  cat("\n")
}
```

Twelve of the 15 $x|x|$ word-space factors have a document-space partner, at
a median cosine of 0.86 --- so where the word search finds a topic, it is one
the document search already found. Nothing is gained. Six document-space
factors have no word-space counterpart, and they are the specific ones: rugby,
law and civil liberties, the Chelsea football factor, television, the
WorldCom fraud, developing-world aid. For `exp_fixed` the loss is far larger,
16 of 24.

## Reproducibility

```{r words-repro}
t(sapply(cts2, function(ct) count_row(getw, ct)))
```

For $x|x|$, 9 of 15 factors are matched in both halves and 10 of a possible
13 pairs match between the halves --- a rate of 0.77, slightly better than
the 0.75 of the document search at the same $K$, at a median cosine of 0.88.
So the word search is not unstable; it simply finds fewer and coarser
topics. `exp_fixed` is a different story: 3 of 10 matched in both halves and
3 of a possible 5 between them.

One caveat on the search budget. The $x|x|$ word runs finish with a worst
`1 - |cos|` of about $5\times10^{-5}$ against roughly $10^{-15}$ in document
mode, so 500 iterations is only marginally enough; `exp_fixed`, which stops
on a tolerance, reached $10^{-8}$ everywhere. Worth raising before leaning on
the $x|x|$ numbers, though it would not explain the `exp_fixed` collapse.

Overall, searching over words is not a good substitute for searching over
documents on this data: $x|x|$ recovers a subset of the same topics and adds
nothing, and the exponential prior largely fails.

# Follow-up: EBproj as an initialization for a topic model

A different use for the EBproj solution: as a starting point for a Poisson
NMF on the **raw counts**. EBproj works on a centred, whitened,
$\log(1 + X/s)$ matrix and returns signed factors; the topic model works on
the counts themselves and returns non-negative ones. If the EBproj maxima are
picking out real structure, they should be a good place to start the topic
model from.

The normalized memberships of the $K = 80$ `exp_fixed` fit on the full data
--- the positive part of the posterior means, each column scaled to a maximum
of 1, i.e. exactly what the structure plots show --- are used as the loadings
initialization for `fastTopics::fit_poisson_nmf`, floored at $10^{-4}$ so no
document is stuck at zero. There are 24 of them, so $k = 24$. The same fit is
then run from fastTopics' own default initialization, 500 SCD iterations
each. Compute is in
[`code/fit_bbc_fasttopics.R`](https://github.com/stephenslab/misc/blob/master/code/fit_bbc_fasttopics.R).

```{r ft-load}
library(fastTopics)
ft <- readRDS("../output/bbc_fasttopics_K80.rds")
ef <- get("full", "exp_fixed")
A  <- ft$A_init; colnames(A) <- colnames(ef$L)
M  <- list(ebproj = poisson2multinom(ft$ebp)$L,
           default = poisson2multinom(ft$def)$L)
ft_words <- function(fit, j, n = 8)
  paste(ft$terms[order(-fit$F[, j])[1:n]], collapse = ", ")
ft_name <- function(fit)
  make.unique(apply(fit$F, 2, function(f)
    paste(ft$terms[order(-f)[1:2]], collapse = "/")))
for (k in names(M)) colnames(M[[k]]) <- ft_name(ft[[c(ebproj = "ebp",
                                                      default = "def")[k]]])
```

## The EBproj start reaches a better optimum

```{r ft-loglik}
c(`EBproj-initialized` = round(ft$loglik_ebp, 1),
  `default init`       = round(ft$loglik_def, 1),
  difference           = round(ft$loglik_ebp - ft$loglik_def, 1))
```

Same $k$, same iteration budget, same method, and the two runs took the same
time (1.9 minutes each). Starting from the EBproj memberships gains about
1350 log-likelihood units. That is not a small reordering of the same answer:
20 of the 24 topics are mutual nearest neighbours across the two fits (median
membership correlation 0.88), and four are unique to each. The four the
EBproj start finds and the default does not are television
(`show, bbc, broadcast, programm, televis`), government and public services,
corporate share and stock, and digital music (`music, digit, gadget, appl,
download`) --- the first and last being topics the EBproj fit itself has. The
default run instead splits off two rather diffuse factors
(`peopl, time, thing, make, work, good` and
`peopl, search, hunt, inform, blog, onlin`).

## Structure plots for the two fits {.tabset}

Topic proportions, so every bar is full height by construction --- unlike the
EBproj structure plots earlier, where the bar height carried information.

```{r ft-struct, results='asis', fig.width=10, fig.height=4}
for (k in names(M)) {
  cat(sprintf("\n### %s\n\n", c(ebproj = "initialized from EBproj",
                                  default = "default initialization")[k]))
  print(plot_struct(M[[k]], TRUE, sprintf("topic model, %s init", k)))
  cat("\n")
}
```

## {-}

## Memberships against the initialization

Comparing memberships rather than word loadings is the fairer test here: the
EBproj word loadings are fitted **with an intercept**, so they measure
departure from the corpus average, whereas the topic model has no intercept
and its $F$ is an absolute word distribution. The document memberships carry
no such asymmetry --- both are non-negative per-document weights on a topic
--- so they can be correlated directly.

```{r ft-membership, results='asis'}
mm <- mnn(cor(A, M$ebproj))
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  `EBproj factor` = colnames(A),
  topic = ifelse(mm$mutual, paste0("t", mm$j), "-"),
  r     = fmt(ifelse(mm$mutual, mm$cos, NA)),
  `top words of the topic` = ifelse(mm$mutual,
    sapply(mm$j, function(j) ft_words(ft$ebp, j)), "-"),
  check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "EBproj memberships against the fitted topic proportions")
```

```{r ft-membership-summary}
t(sapply(names(M), function(k) {
  m <- mnn(cor(A, M[[k]]))
  c(`mutual pairs` = sum(m$mutual), `of` = ncol(A),
    `median r` = round(median(m$cos[m$mutual]), 2),
    `min r` = round(min(m$cos[m$mutual]), 2),
    `max r` = round(max(m$cos[m$mutual]), 2))
}))
```

Nineteen of the 24 EBproj factors survive into the fitted topic model as a
mutual nearest neighbour, at a median membership correlation of 0.77. The
strong ones are the large, distinctive topics --- tennis at 0.94, rugby 0.93,
athletics 0.91, music 0.91, television 0.87, video games 0.86 --- and the
weak one is doping (`test/athlet`) at 0.36, which the topic model apparently
absorbs into a broader sport topic. Five EBproj factors have no mutual
partner at all: the `number/top` box-office axis, the tax-and-spend politics
factor, the dollar and trade deficit, the football match report, and the
WorldCom fraud.

### Everything found by any of the three

One row per topic across the union of the EBproj initialization and the two
topic model fits, anchored on the EBproj factors, with any topic that no
EBproj factor claims added below. Each of the three columns holds the
membership correlation where the topic is present and `-` where it is not, so
the columns double as presence indicators. Key words come from the
EBproj-initialized topic model where the row appears in it, otherwise from
the default fit, otherwise from the EBproj word loadings.

```{r ft-union}
me <- mnn(cor(A, M$ebproj)); md <- mnn(cor(A, M$default))
ie <- ifelse(me$mutual, me$j, NA); id <- ifelse(md$mutual, md$j, NA)
med <- mnn(cor(M$ebproj, M$default))

# Topics that no EBproj factor claimed, paired with each other where mutual.
le <- setdiff(seq_len(ncol(M$ebproj)), na.omit(ie))
ld <- setdiff(seq_len(ncol(M$default)), na.omit(id))
je <- ifelse(med$mutual[le] & med$j[le] %in% ld, med$j[le], NA)
ld <- setdiff(ld, na.omit(je))
xe <- c(le, rep(NA, length(ld))); xd <- c(je, ld)

n_eb <- ncol(A); n_x <- length(xe)
col_e <- c(ie, xe); col_d <- c(id, xd)          # topic index per row, or NA

# Row label: the EBproj factor name, or the topic's own name if EBproj has no
# such factor.
lbl <- c(colnames(A),
         ifelse(!is.na(xe), colnames(M$ebproj)[pmax(xe, 1)],
                colnames(M$default)[pmax(xd, 1)]))

# Key words: from the EBproj-initialized fit where the row is in it, else the
# default fit, else the EBproj word loadings.
kw <- ifelse(!is.na(col_e),
             sapply(pmax(col_e, 1), function(j) ft_words(ft$ebp, j)),
      ifelse(!is.na(col_d),
             sapply(pmax(col_d, 1), function(j) ft_words(ft$def, j)),
             c(sapply(seq_len(n_eb), function(j) top_words(efx, j, 8)),
               rep("", n_x))))

# A correlation where the row has an EBproj factor to correlate against,
# "present" where it does not, "-" where the fit lacks the topic entirely.
tab <- data.frame(
  factor = lbl,
  EBproj = c(rep("yes", n_eb), rep("-", n_x)),
  `topic: EBproj init` = c(fmt(ifelse(me$mutual, me$cos, NA)),
                           ifelse(is.na(xe), "-", "present")),
  `topic: default`     = c(fmt(ifelse(md$mutual, md$cos, NA)),
                           ifelse(is.na(xd), "-", "present")),
  `key words` = kw, check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(tab, row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Union of the EBproj factors and the topics of the two fits")
```

```{r ft-union-counts}
c(`EBproj factors` = ncol(A),
  `topics, EBproj init` = ncol(M$ebproj),
  `topics, default` = ncol(M$default),
  `rows in the union` = nrow(tab),
  `in all three` = sum(tab$EBproj == "yes" &
                         tab$`topic: EBproj init` != "-" &
                         tab$`topic: default` != "-"))
```

Across the three there are 33 distinct topics, of which 16 appear in all
three and nine are found by only one. The EBproj-only ones are the four
listed above plus `chelsea/club`, which both topic models find only loosely
(0.66 and 0.64). Going the other way, the default fit contributes four topics
neither of the others has, and two of them --- `peopl, time, thing, make,
work, good` and `peopl, search, hunt, inform, blog, onlin` --- are the
diffuse factors noted earlier, so the extra topics it finds are the weaker
ones.

Two caveats on reading this as "the initialization persisted". First, the
correspondence is one of *topics*, not of column indices: only `L` is
supplied, so `F` starts random and the topic labels shuffle in the first few
updates. Second, and more importantly, the default fit agrees with the EBproj
memberships about as well as the EBproj-initialized fit does --- 17 mutual
pairs at median 0.77, against 19 at 0.77. Much of that agreement is therefore
just both topic models finding the same structure the EBproj factors describe,
not a trace of the starting point. **The benefit of the initialization shows
up in the likelihood and in which topics get separated, not in the
memberships being closer to where they started.**

Worth noting how different the starting point is from what fastTopics would
normally be given: the EBproj memberships are 84.5% exactly zero, with a
median of 30 documents above 0.5 per factor. It is a far sparser and more
committed initialization than `topicscore` produces, which is presumably why
it lands in a different basin.

# Next steps

* The $K$ sweep is now two points, 40 and 80, and they disagree about which
  is better: $K = 40$ is far more reproducible at every contrast, $K = 80$
  finds roughly twice as many topics. Filling in 50--60 would say whether the
  reproducibility falls off gradually or has a knee.
* Repeat the split under a few different seeds. One split is enough to rank
  the three contrasts --- the ordering 0.75 / 0.64 / 0.31 is not close ---
  but not to put an error bar on any single rate.
* $x^3$ is the most interesting of the three and the least stable. Worth
  asking whether its extra factors can be filtered rather than avoided: they
  are individually checkable against the half-split, and the ones that
  survive (19 of 36) include several the other contrasts never find.
* Compare against the log1p NMF fits of Weine et al. at the same $K$, which
  is the actual point of using this corpus. Fits at $c = 0.001$ and
  $K = 10, 40$ are already in `output/`.
* Try the point-exponential prior, which estimates $\pi_0$, $c$ and
  $\sigma^2$ rather than fixing them. The word-space result below suggests
  the fixed scale $c^2 = 1/2$ is doing real work, since relaxing the search
  to a space where it fits badly is where `exp_fixed` collapses.
